Implement Task 16 ("Reel scenes in the Loupe direction") from docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-product.md.

Read first: that plan's Task 16 in full; the Global Constraints of docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-core.md; Task 6 of the core plan (the renderer you are restyling); and the current code in packages/reel/src. If the remotion-best-practices and frontend-design skills are available, use them.

The visual target is a set of seven static reference frames at /Users/yehor/Desktop/projects/neathack-internal/finalists/03-loupe/ : open frames.html and the images frame-1.png to frame-7.png (title, prompt, terminal, diff, stats, flag, end) and study them before you write anything. Read only inside that directory. They show the composition, the lens, the film strip and the pencil marks at the quality expected. Your job is to make the real renderer produce frames that hold up next to them, from real storyboard data of any length, and to add what a still cannot show: the lens gliding from scene to scene and the pencil marks drawing on.

This is the part of the product people will actually see. Spend your effort on how the frames look and move. Look at your own rendered stills often, and be honest about which ones are weaker than the reference.

Keep the render API and the timeline behaviour exactly as they are; other packages call them. The one schema change is the optional `unverified` field on the end scene, as the task says.

There is no `.env` and there are no API keys in this checkout, by design. Rendering needs the network for fonts and a browser download; that is expected.

Commit after each green test cycle. Finish by running the reel package's tests and `pnpm typecheck` at the repo root.

End with a short report: what exists now, test counts, which frames you consider weakest and why, and every deviation from the plan with the reason.

Implement Task 16 ("Reel scenes in the Loupe direction") from docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-product.md.

Read first: that plan's Task 16 in full; the Global Constraints of docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-core.md; Task 6 of the core plan (the renderer you are restyling); and the current code in packages/reel/src. If the remotion-best-practices and frontend-design skills are available, use them.

The visual target is a set of seven static reference frames at /Users/yehor/Desktop/projects/neathack-internal/finalists/03-loupe/ : open frames.html and the images frame-1.png to frame-7.png (title, prompt, terminal, diff, stats, flag, end) and study them before you write anything. Read only inside that directory. They show the composition, the lens, the film strip and the pencil marks at the quality expected. Your job is to make the real renderer produce frames that hold up next to them, from real storyboard data of any length, and to add what a still cannot show: the lens gliding from scene to scene and the pencil marks drawing on.

This is the part of the product people will actually see. Spend your effort on how the frames look and move. Look at your own rendered stills often, and be honest about which ones are weaker than the reference.

Keep the render API and the timeline behaviour exactly as they are; other packages call them. The one schema change is the optional `unverified` field on the end scene, as the task says.

There is no `.env` and there are no API keys in this checkout, by design. Rendering needs the network for fonts and a browser download; that is expected.

Commit after each green test cycle. Finish by running the reel package's tests and `pnpm typecheck` at the repo root.

End with a short report: what exists now, test counts, which frames you consider weakest and why, and every deviation from the plan with the reason.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.

6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. - Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:

    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Dailies Product Layer Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Put the core pipeline behind a web API with a background worker, measure the verifier on real data, and let the agent read its own trace history at run time.

**Architecture:** `apps/web` is a Next.js app that only reads and writes SQLite rows and serves files. A separate worker process executes runs with the durable runner. `eval/` holds benchmarks that reuse `@dailies/ingest` and `@dailies/verify` unchanged. `@dailies/agent` gains a small client for the neatlogs MCP endpoint.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js (App Router, route handlers), better-sqlite3, the packages from the core plan, vitest.

**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md` (sections 5, 6, 7, 9). Builds on `docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-core.md`; its Global Constraints apply here unchanged.

## Global Constraints

- Everything in the core plan's Global Constraints.
- The web app never imports `@dailies/reel`, `@remotion/*`, `openai` or `neatlogs`. Rendering and model calls happen only in the worker.
- The worker runs one pipeline at a time.
- No API key is needed to run any test in this plan. Live checks are separate scripts that exit with a clear message when a key is missing.
- Evaluation results never name a repository. Repositories are identified by the first 8 hex characters of the SHA-256 of their URL.

## Review Focus

1. Two requests create runs for the same repository at once: both are accepted and executed one after the other; neither corrupts the other's artifacts. Pinned in Task 11.
2. A client disconnects from the event stream mid-run: the server stops polling for it and the run is unaffected. Pinned in Task 11.
3. A request asks for `/media/<run>/../../.env`: rejected with 400 before touching the filesystem. Pinned in Task 11.
4. A real test-runner output the parser has never seen: counted as `unknown` in the recognition rate, never as a pass. Pinned in Task 12.
5. The neatlogs endpoint is down or returns a non-JSON body: the run proceeds without history and records `memory: skipped`. Pinned in Task 13.

## Task order

Tasks 11, 12 and 13 are independent of each other and of core Tasks 8 and 9. Task 11 needs core Task 7 merged; Task 12 needs core Tasks 2 and 4; Task 13 needs core Task 3. Task 14 needs Task 11 and the chosen visual direction.

1	# Dailies Core Implementation Plan
2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
4	
5	**Goal:** From a repository URL, produce a fact-checked, narrated MP4 reel of its recorded coding-agent sessions through a resumable pipeline and a CLI.
6	
7	**Architecture:** A pnpm TypeScript monorepo. `packages/core` holds every shared schema; each other package exposes plain functions over those schemas. A durable runner executes stages in order and persists each stage's artifact so a run can resume.
8	
9	**Tech Stack:** Node 22+, pnpm workspaces, TypeScript (strict, ESM), zod, vitest, OpenAI SDK against an OpenAI-compatible gateway, neatlogs SDK, Remotion 4, better-sqlite3, ffmpeg, git, Entire CLI.
10	
11	**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md`
12	
13	This plan covers Tier 1 of the spec. The web app, evaluation harness, runtime read-back and deployment are separate plans that build on the interfaces fixed here.
14	
15	## Global Constraints
16	
17	- Node `>=22`. TypeScript `strict: true`, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
18	- Internal packages are consumed as TypeScript source: `"exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" }`. No build step; run with `tsx`, check with `tsc --noEmit`.
19	- Package names: `@dailies/core`, `@dailies/ingest`, `@dailies/agent`, `@dailies/verify`, `@dailies/voice`, `@dailies/reel`, `@dailies/pipeline`, `@dailies/cli`.
20	- A package imports another only through its index. Shared types live in `@dailies/core` and nowhere else.
21	- A task edits files only inside the directories listed under its **Files**. Do not change another package's `package.json`.
22	- Tests: vitest, files `packages/<name>/test/*.test.ts`. Run one package with `pnpm --filter @dailies/<name> test`.
23	- No secret ever enters the repository. Configuration comes from `.env` through `loadEnv()`.
24	- Every model call goes through `@dailies/agent`. No other package imports `openai`.
25	- Model ids on the gateway: `claude-sonnet-4.6`, `claude-haiku`, `nova-pro`. Gateway base URL: `LITELLM_BASE_URL`. Stay under 50 requests per minute.
26	- Trace endpoint: `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
27	- A verdict is `verified` only on positive evidence. Anything unknown is `unverifiable`, never `verified` and never `contradicted`.
28	- Commit after every green test cycle with a short imperative message.
29	- Once code exists, locate it with `entire graph search` before broad grep, as `CLAUDE.md` instructs.
30	
31	## Review Focus
32	
33	1. A repository with no checkpoints, or none inside the window: the run ends early with a clear message and no render. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 10.
34	2. A tool result of several megabytes or with ANSI colour codes: entries are truncated head-and-tail, colour codes are stripped, memory stays flat. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 4.
35	3. A claim quote that differs from the transcript only by whitespace or Markdown marks: still matched. A quote that is not in the entry: dropped. Pinned in Task 4.
36	4. A test run whose output the parser does not recognise: `unknown`, so the claim is `unverifiable`. Pinned in Task 4.
37	5. Narration audio whose pause count does not equal the line count: timings fall back to proportional alignment and never throw. Pinned in Task 5.
38	6. A model reply that is not valid JSON for the schema: one repair turn, then the stage fails and the runner retries it. Pinned in Task 3.
39	7. A secret inside a human prompt or a tool result: redacted at ingest, before any model or renderer sees it. Pinned in Task 1 and Task 2.
40	
41	## File Structure
42	
43	```
44	package.json  pnpm-workspace.yaml  tsconfig.base.json  vitest.config.ts  .nvmrc
45	packages/core/src/      schema.ts ids.ts redact.ts env.ts budget.ts facts.ts index.ts
46	packages/ingest/src/    git.ts checkpoints.ts transcript.ts trailers.ts window.ts index.ts
47	packages/agent/src/     router.ts meter.ts limiter.ts loop.ts tools.ts trace.ts mock.ts index.ts
48	packages/verify/src/    commands.ts results.ts rules.ts quote.ts ground.ts style.ts index.ts
49	packages/voice/src/     gemini.ts wav.ts silence.ts align.ts index.ts
50	packages/reel/src/      timeline.ts srt.ts theme.ts render.ts index.ts

# Dailies Core Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** From a repository URL, produce a fact-checked, narrated MP4 reel of its recorded coding-agent sessions through a resumable pipeline and a CLI.

**Architecture:** A pnpm TypeScript monorepo. `packages/core` holds every shared schema; each other package exposes plain functions over those schemas. A durable runner executes stages in order and persists each stage's artifact so a run can resume.

**Tech Stack:** Node 22+, pnpm workspaces, TypeScript (strict, ESM), zod, vitest, OpenAI SDK against an OpenAI-compatible gateway, neatlogs SDK, Remotion 4, better-sqlite3, ffmpeg, git, Entire CLI.

**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md`

This plan covers Tier 1 of the spec. The web app, evaluation harness, runtime read-back and deployment are separate plans that build on the interfaces fixed here.

## Global Constraints

- Node `>=22`. TypeScript `strict: true`, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
- Internal packages are consumed as TypeScript source: `"exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" }`. No build step; run with `tsx`, check with `tsc --noEmit`.
- Package names: `@dailies/core`, `@dailies/ingest`, `@dailies/agent`, `@dailies/verify`, `@dailies/voice`, `@dailies/reel`, `@dailies/pipeline`, `@dailies/cli`.
- A package imports another only through its index. Shared types live in `@dailies/core` and nowhere else.
- A task edits files only inside the directories listed under its **Files**. Do not change another package's `package.json`.
- Tests: vitest, files `packages/<name>/test/*.test.ts`. Run one package with `pnpm --filter @dailies/<name> test`.
- No secret ever enters the repository. Configuration comes from `.env` through `loadEnv()`.
- Every model call goes through `@dailies/agent`. No other package imports `openai`.
- Model ids on the gateway: `claude-sonnet-4.6`, `claude-haiku`, `nova-pro`. Gateway base URL: `LITELLM_BASE_URL`. Stay under 50 requests per minute.
- Trace endpoint: `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
- A verdict is `verified` only on positive evidence. Anything unknown is `unverifiable`, never `verified` and never `contradicted`.
- Commit after every green test cycle with a short imperative message.
- Once code exists, locate it with `entire graph search` before broad grep, as `CLAUDE.md` instructs.

## Review Focus

1. A repository with no checkpoints, or none inside the window: the run ends early with a clear message and no render. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 10.
2. A tool result of several megabytes or with ANSI colour codes: entries are truncated head-and-tail, colour codes are stripped, memory stays flat. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 4.
3. A claim quote that differs from the transcript only by whitespace or Markdown marks: still matched. A quote that is not in the entry: dropped. Pinned in Task 4.
4. A test run whose output the parser does not recognise: `unknown`, so the claim is `unverifiable`. Pinned in Task 4.
5. Narration audio whose pause count does not equal the line count: timings fall back to proportional alignment and never throw. Pinned in Task 5.
6. A model reply that is not valid JSON for the schema: one repair turn, then the stage fails and the runner retries it. Pinned in Task 3.
7. A secret inside a human prompt or a tool result: redacted at ingest, before any model or renderer sees it. Pinned in Task 1 and Task 2.

## File Structure

```
package.json  pnpm-workspace.yaml  tsconfig.base.json  vitest.config.ts  .nvmrc
packages/core/src/      schema.ts ids.ts redact.ts env.ts budget.ts facts.ts index.ts
packages/ingest/src/    git.ts checkpoints.ts transcript.ts trailers.ts window.ts index.ts
packages/agent/src/     router.ts meter.ts limiter.ts loop.ts tools.ts trace.ts mock.ts index.ts
packages/verify/src/    commands.ts results.ts rules.ts quote.ts ground.ts style.ts index.ts
packages/voice/src/     gemini.ts wav.ts silence.ts align.ts index.ts
packages/reel/src/      timeline.ts srt.ts theme.ts render.ts index.ts
packages/reel/src/remotion/   index.ts Root.tsx Reel.tsx scenes/*.tsx
packages/pipeline/src/  db.ts store.ts runner.ts types.ts index.ts
packages/pipeline/src/stages/   ingest.ts edit.ts verify.ts script.ts ground.ts voice.ts render.ts review.ts gate.ts
packages/pipeline/src/prompts/  editor.ts extractor.ts judge.ts writer.ts entail.ts reviewer.ts
packages/cli/src/       index.ts run.ts verify.ts
packages/cli/bin/       dailies entire-dailies
```

## Task order

Task 1 first, alone. Then Tasks 2–7 in parallel, each in its own worktree. Then Tasks 8 and 9 in parallel. Then Task 10.

701	### Task 6: Reel renderer
702	
703	**Files:** `packages/reel/src/**`, `packages/reel/test/**`
704	
705	**Interfaces:**
706	- Consumes: `Storyboard`, `Scene`, `LineTiming`, `RenderArtifact` from `@dailies/core`.
707	- Produces:
708	```ts
709	export interface Timeline { fps: number; totalFrames: number; audioStartFrame: number; scenes: { sceneId: string; startFrame: number; durationInFrames: number }[] }
710	export function buildTimeline(sb: Storyboard, timings: LineTiming[], fps?: number): Timeline
711	export function toSrt(sb: Storyboard, timings: LineTiming[], audioOffsetSec: number): string
712	export async function renderReel(i: { storyboard: Storyboard; timings: LineTiming[]; audioPath: string | null; outDir: string }): Promise<RenderArtifact>
713	export async function renderStills(i: { storyboard: Storyboard; timings: LineTiming[]; outDir: string }): Promise<{ sceneId: string; path: string }[]>
714	```
715	
716	Behaviour:
717	
718	- **Timeline.** 30 fps. The title scene lasts 2.5 s and plays before the narration; `audioStartFrame` is its length. Each spoken scene starts at the start of its first line and ends at the start of the next spoken scene's first line; the last spoken scene ends at the end of its last line plus 0.4 s. The end scene lasts 3 s. Scene frames are contiguous and `totalFrames` is their sum. A line with no timing, or a storyboard that is not a title, spoken scenes and an end, throws rather than rendering out of sync. Cut points are kept at least one frame apart, so colliding timings still give every scene a positive length.
719	- **Subtitles.** One cue per line, shifted by `audioOffsetSec`, `HH:MM:SS,mmm` timestamps.
720	- **Rendering.** `bundle({ entryPoint: <src/remotion/index.ts>, publicDir: <outDir>/public })` with the narration copied to `public/narration.wav`; `selectComposition({ id: 'Reel', inputProps })`; `renderMedia({ codec: 'h264', outputLocation: <outDir>/reel.mp4 })`. The poster is `renderStill` at the middle of the title scene. `renderReel` writes `reel.mp4`, `reel.srt` and `poster.png` into `outDir` and returns absolute paths. `renderStills` writes one PNG per scene at that scene's middle frame, named `NN-<type>.png` in scene order; the review stage uses them. Its signature carries no audio flag, so stills are always drawn as the captions cut: that is the tighter layout and shows every piece of text a frame can carry.
721	- **Composition.** `Reel.tsx` maps each timeline scene to a `<Sequence>` and switches on `scene.type`. Audio is one `<Audio src={staticFile('narration.wav')}>` inside a `<Sequence from={audioStartFrame}>`, omitted when there is no audio. In captions mode the current line's text is drawn as a caption bar.
722	- **Scenes.** One component per scene type in `src/remotion/scenes/`. All colours, type sizes, radii and font families come from `theme.ts`; no scene hard-codes a visual value, so the art direction can change in one file. Text is clamped to the limits the schema already enforces. Motion uses `interpolate` and `spring` only. Shared pieces sit beside the scenes: `text.ts` (pure clamping, fitting, diff and count-up helpers, unit-tested), `ui.tsx` (frame, motion helpers), `config.ts` (composition id and props, importable from Node).
723	  - `Title`: repo name, window label, session and commit counts.
724	  - `Prompt`: the quoted human prompt, typed on.
725	  - `Terminal`: commands and outputs revealed step by step, a pass or fail mark per step.
726	  - `Diff`: the patch with added and removed lines coloured, counters for both.
727	  - `Stats`: up to six labelled values counting up.
728	  - `Flag`: the agent's quote, the verdict stamp, the recorded reality.
729	  - `End`: repo, verified and flagged counts.
730	  - Two rules tie the theme to the review stage (Task 9), and `theme.test.ts` pins both. Every entrance has landed before the middle of its scene (`theme.motion.settleBy` below 0.5), because that is the frame `renderStills` hands the reviewer; a prompt still being typed there reads as cut-off text. The backdrop keeps a luma of at least 0.12, because the review runs `blackdetect` at its default pixel threshold of 0.10 and a darker background turns every sparse frame into a black segment, which blocks the run.
731	  - Text is fitted by estimated glyph width, not character count, so a Cyrillic or CJK quote shrinks instead of overflowing. In captions mode every scene keeps a bottom inset free for a three-line caption bar.

export const COMMENT = (what) => `<!--
Dailies — 03 Loupe — ${what}
direction: one frame of the night's footage under an illuminated loupe on a switched-off lightbox. The only lit thing in the room is the frame that matters.
anchor: a photo editor's 4x illuminated loupe (Peak / Schneider) on 35mm stock; Magnum contact-sheet practice of marking selects in grease pencil.
fonts: Unbounded (display) / Figtree (text) / Martian Mono (mono, width axis 75 for code)
colour scale:
  lightbox-950 #0d1211  page, far field        emulsion-950 #070a09  film base, unlit
  lightbox-900 #121917  lightbox glass          emulsion-800 #131c19  film picture area, unlit
  lightbox-850 #1a2421  near field, light spill emulsion-700 #26352f  film picture area, lit
  glass-400    #8fa099  muted text              emulsion-500 #5b6f68  lightbox through a perforation
  glass-200    #c3cfca  secondary text          white-50     #eef3f1  cool white, type and lit detail
  pencil-400   #ffd60a  grease pencil: verdict marks and the one action
spacing scale: 4 8 12 16 24 32 48 72 112
radius scale: 999px (pills, loupe) / 20px (player) / 5px (film picture area) / 2px (perforations)
grammar: film frames are the record. The lens is the check: it sits on a claim and shows the record under it. Pills are what a person does.
  Grease pencil is the verdict, and yellow is used for nothing else but the one action: ring = verified, cross = contradicted, dashed ring = stale, question mark = unverified.
-->`;

Extract the claims the coding agent made, then judge each one.

Extraction: a small model reads assistant messages at turn ends and returns claims with the exact quote and the entry id. A claim is kept only if its quote is found in that entry (compared after collapsing whitespace and Markdown marks).

| Claim kind | Evidence | Verdict rule |
|---|---|---|
| `tests_pass` | last test-runner call in the session before the claim, and its output | verified if it passed; contradicted if it failed; stale if code was edited after the last passing run; unverifiable if no run exists |
| `build_passes` | same for build, type-check and lint commands | same |
| `ran_command` | a matching tool call and its result | verified if it succeeded; contradicted if it errored; unverifiable if no matching call is recorded |
| `fixed_error` | the error text in an earlier tool result and a later run of the same command without it | unverifiable when no later run exists |
| `implemented` | the diff of the linked commits | a second model must quote the supporting hunk; the quote is validated against the diff |

The first four are decided by deterministic parsers over the recorded tool results. Only `implemented` uses a model, from a different model family than the writer, and its quoted evidence is checked mechanically.

**4.4 Script**
The writer produces a storyboard: ordered scenes with typed props and narration lines. The reel follows one arc: the problem (the human's request), the key decisions, the implementation, and the recorded validation. Each line carries evidence refs. Contradicted and stale claims become flag scenes. Unverifiable claims are either left out or stated as unverified.

**4.5 Ground (gate, in code)**
For every line: evidence refs must resolve; every number in the sentence must appear in the facts computed for that scene; a second model must find the sentence entailed by the evidence. A failing line is rewritten up to twice, then dropped. A style lint (banned phrases, sentence length) runs here too. The on-screen text and narration are scanned again for secrets. The stage reports how many lines were dropped.

**4.6 Voice**
Gemini text-to-speech per line, cached by content hash. Measured durations drive the timeline. On failure: retry with backoff, then an alternate voice, then a captions-only cut that is labelled as such.

**4.7 Footage**
Scenes are rendered from data: title, quoted prompt, terminal replay, animated diff, stats, claim-versus-record flag, end card. Tier 3 adds a session timeline, the dependency-graph scene and a Playwright recording of the live app when the repo declares a URL.

**4.8 Render**
Remotion composes the storyboard into 1080p30 MP4, an SRT file and a poster frame.

**4.9 Review (agent)**
Deterministic checks first: total duration against target, silent gaps, black frames, per-scene text limits. Then frames from each scene go to a vision model with a fixed rubric (legibility, overflow, wrong or empty content). Findings map to fixes (shorten a line, change scene parameters, regenerate audio) and the run loops back, at most twice.

**4.10 Gate (in code)**
All must hold: grounding passed, secret scan clean, review passed, cost within budget, human approval recorded. Failure of any condition blocks publishing; there is no override path in the worker.

**4.11 Publish**
9:**Dailies** reads a repository's Entire checkpoints (the recorded coding-agent sessions behind each commit) and produces a 60–90 second narrated video reel of what the agents did. Before it says anything, it checks the agents' claims against the diff and against the tool output recorded in the same session. A claim that the record contradicts becomes an on-screen flag. A sentence the narrator cannot back with evidence is not spoken.

# Dailies design reference: Loupe

The night's work is a strip of film lying on a switched-off lightbox. A loupe moves along it.
What sits under the glass is what the narrator is talking about, and the only lit thing in the
room is the frame that matters.

The anchor is a photo editor's 4× illuminated loupe on 35 mm stock, and the contact-sheet habit
of marking selects in grease pencil. Everything below follows from those two objects.

The reel renderer (`packages/reel`) is the first implementation. Its tokens live in
`packages/reel/src/theme.ts`; nothing under `src/remotion` carries a colour, a size or a family
of its own.

## Colour

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `lightbox.far` | `#0d1211` | the room, far from the lens |
| `lightbox.glass` | `#121917` | the lightbox surface |
| `lightbox.near` | `#1a2421` | light spilling around the lens |
| `film.base` | `#070a09` | unexposed film between and around frames |
| `film.frame` | `#131c19` | a frame's picture area, unlit |
| `film.perf` | `#1c2724` | the lightbox seen through a perforation |
